text: download Thailand national outline GADM save GeoPackage every later notebook can read single st_read() call.
code: # Download Thailand at `level = 0` (= national outline only). # `geodata::gadm()` caches the raw download under `raw_dir`. tha    <- gadm(country = "THA", level = 0, path = raw_dir)  # Convert the SpatVector to an `sf` object — sf is the modern tidy class for # vector spatial data and plays nicely with dplyr. tha_sf <- st_as_sf(tha)  # Save as a GeoPackage (one self-contained file) into the boundary sub-folder. st_write(tha_sf,          file.path(boundary_dir, "thailand_boundary.gpkg"),          delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)  plot(st_geometry(tha_sf), main = "Thailand boundary (GADM level 0)")

code: # Download the global WorldClim v2.1 bioclim stack (19 layers). bio_global <- worldclim_global(var = "bio", res = 10, path = raw_dir)  # Restrict the global stack to Thailand: #   crop() trims the raster to Thailand's bounding box (the rectangle) #   mask() sets every pixel *outside* the country polygon to NA bio_tha <- crop(bio_global, terra::ext(tha)) bio_tha <- mask(bio_tha, tha)  # Tidy the layer names so they read as `bio1` ... `bio19` instead of the # verbose WorldClim default (`wc2.1_10m_bio_1`, ...). The vignettes refer to # the variables by these short names. names(bio_tha) <- paste0("bio", seq_len(terra::nlyr(bio_tha)))  # Save the 19-band raster as a single multi-band GeoTIFF. writeRaster(   bio_tha,   filename  = file.path(bioclim_dir, "bioclim_thailand.tif"),   overwrite = TRUE )  # Re-read from disk so what we plot is exactly what later notebooks will see. bio_tha <- rast(file.path(bioclim_dir, "bioclim_thailand.tif"))  plot(bio_tha[[c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15")]],      main = c("BIO1 — mean T (°C)",               "BIO12 — annual precip. (mm)",               "BIO15 — precip. seasonality (CV)"))

OBSERVATION — generic observation record, less specific HUMAN_OBSERVATION. Still field record, keep . OCCURRENCE — catch-“species time” record. include excluding discard otherwise usable field data. exclude categories represent contemporary, wild, -situ animals: FOSSIL_SPECIMEN — animal lived long ago; relevant today’s climate niche. PRESERVED_SPECIMEN — museum herbarium material; locality information often skewed toward roads, towns, historical expeditions. LIVING_SPECIMEN — captive animals zoos breeding centres; location says nothing wild niche. title: Pre-workshop — Downloading and preparing the workshop data
text: loop three basisOfRecord categories kept, calling rgbif::occ_search() per category concatenating results. also ask GBIF return records already coordinates flagged geospatial issues — saves us cleaning round later.
code: allowed_basis <- c("HUMAN_OBSERVATION", "OCCURRENCE", "OBSERVATION")  # Query GBIF once per basisOfRecord category. `lapply()` returns a list of # data frames, one per category, which we then row-bind into a single table. raw_list <- lapply(allowed_basis, function(b) {   rgbif::occ_search(     taxonKey           = key,         # unique taxon identifier from Sub-step 2     country            = "TH",        # ISO-2 country code for Thailand     basisOfRecord      = b,           # this category only     hasCoordinate      = TRUE,        # drop records without lon/lat     hasGeospatialIssue = FALSE,       # drop records with known coord problems     limit              = 5000         # generous upper bound per category   )$data })  raw <- dplyr::bind_rows(raw_list)  # Belt-and-braces: re-apply the basisOfRecord filter on the combined table # in case the API quietly returns something we did not ask for. raw <- raw %>% filter(basisOfRecord %in% allowed_basis)  # Save the raw download to disk so we have a snapshot we can re-read later # without re-hitting GBIF. write_csv(raw, file.path(gbif_dir, "sambar_gbif.csv"))  nrow(raw)

what: Sub-step 4 — Clean the table and keep only points inside Thailand
title: Pre-workshop — Downloading and preparing the workshop data
text: GBIF tags records country observed , polygon plot precise. Coordinates labelled country = "TH" can still fall kilometres offshore (e.g. island sightings, GPS error). filter spatially Thailand polygon sure every record actually lies Thai land.
code: # Re-read the raw snapshot we just wrote. sambar <- read_csv(file.path(gbif_dir, "sambar_gbif.csv"))  # Keep only the columns we will need downstream and drop rows with missing # coordinates (we already asked GBIF for `hasCoordinate = TRUE`, but a final # sanity check is cheap). sambar <- raw %>%   select(species,          decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude,          year, month,          basisOfRecord, gbifID) %>%   filter(!is.na(decimalLongitude),          !is.na(decimalLatitude),          basisOfRecord %in% allowed_basis)  # Turn the table into spatial points (CRS 4326 = WGS84 longitude/latitude). # `remove = FALSE` keeps the numeric lon/lat columns alongside the geometry. sambar_sf <- st_as_sf(sambar,                       coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),                       crs    = 4326,                       remove = FALSE)  # Test which records actually fall inside the Thailand polygon. `st_within()` # returns a one-column logical matrix, so we pull out column 1. inside  <- st_within(sambar_sf, tha_sf, sparse = FALSE)[, 1] sambar  <- sambar[inside, ]

Together three windows describe small, well-defined ellipsoid sitting lowland, seasonally-wet corner Thailand’s environmental space. Printing ell shows compact summary niche. Reading output line line: Dimensions: 3D. Three environmental axes, ellipsoid true 3-D shape (“egg” BIO1 × BIO12 × BIO15 space). Chi-square cutoff: 11.345. 95% probability boundary niche, taken chi-square distribution 3 degrees freedom. Pixels squared Mahalanobis distance cutoff fall inside niche; rest outside. Centroid (mu): (26.5, 1850, 80). geometric centre ranges — preferred environmental conditions. Covariance matrix. diagonal matrix three ranges specified independently — axis varies cross-axis covariances zero. Ellipsoid semi-axis lengths: 729.78, 11.227, 1.684. half-widths ellipsoid direction. Notice stretched bio12 axis (precipitation values span hundreds mm) compared bio15 (CV values span tens) — ellipsoid elongated along precipitation. Ellipsoid axis endpoints. two vertex coordinates ends axis — useful sanity-checking ellipsoid actually reaches ranges specified. Ellipsoid volume: 57 800.1. total amount E-space niche occupies, mixed units. Useful comparing niche breadths species. can visualise ellipsoid E-space cloud environmental conditions Thailand actually offers — background point cloud. Every grey dot one pixel country plotted BIO1 × BIO12 (third axis, BIO15, collapsed 2-D view). niche sits inside cloud can realised geographically; niche sits outside cloud produce empty suitability map.  ellipse plot 2-D projection niche onto BIO1 × BIO12 plane. grey dots background point cloud. code: sp_rich_layer   <- rast("data/processed/bias/sp_richness_TH.tif") nighttime_layer <- rast("data/processed/bias/nighttime_TH.tif")  # Stack the two proxies into a 2-layer SpatRaster and rename for clarity. bias_layer <- c(sp_rich_layer, nighttime_layer) names(bias_layer) <- c("sp_richness", "nighttime_light") plot(bias_layer) # prepare_bias() rescales each proxy to 0-1, optionally inverts proxies whose # *high* values represent *low* sampling effort, and combines the two into a # single composite surface. `effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse")` # tells it to use richness directly but invert night-time lights. bias_prep <- prepare_bias(   bias_surface     = bias_layer,   effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse") )  # The composite surface is a 0-1 map of "how likely a survey would happen # here": high values mark accessible, biodiversity-rich pixels; low values # mark remote, brightly-lit-but-empty pixels (essentially, urban areas). plot(bias_prep$composite_surface) biased_pred <- apply_bias(   prepared_bias    = bias_prep,                 # the composite bias surface from prepare_bias()   prediction       = pred,                      # the projected ellipsoid from predict()   prediction_layer = "suitability",             # which layer of `pred` to multiply against bias   effect_direction = "direct"                   # high bias → high realised sampling )  par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(pred$suitability,      main = "Unbiased suitability") plot(biased_pred$suitability_biased,      main = "Suitability × bias = realised sampling surface") par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

text: find_env_resolution() derives grid resolution thinning directly data. per variable, meaning returns one suggested cell width environmental axis (BIO1 gets width, BIO12 gets different width, BIO15 gets yet another), natural units variable. widths come kernel-density bandwidth variable’s marginal distribution: bandwidth scale, two occurrences carry essentially environmental information, natural cell width extra records redundant. Three classic bandwidth selectors supported: "sheather-jones" (default) — Sheather & Jones (1991) plug-selector; robust non-Gaussian shapes modern recommended default. "silverman" — Silverman’s rule thumb; fast stable distribution roughly Gaussian. "scott" — Scott’s rule; Gaussian-optimal variant Silverman. Sheather–Jones fails (can happen strongly tied data) function automatically falls back Silverman’s rule variable emits message. run three selectors compare , pick one feed thinning step. Read across row compare. Silverman Scott simple plug-ins assume roughly Gaussian distribution, usually return similar, slightly larger bandwidths, coarser cells, fewer pods, aggressive thinning. Sheather–Jones data-adaptive usually smaller, finer cells, pods, gentler thinning. real occurrence data, almost never Gaussian, recommend "sheather-jones": preserves environmental nuance safest default workshop. method’s diagnostic plot. panel kernel-density estimate (KDE) one bioclim variable; red horizontal scale bar marks bandwidth selector chose — .e. suggested cell width.    Reading panels: black curve kernel-density estimate occurrence points distributed along environmental axis; shaded area curve helps eye see bulk density sits; red horizontal bar suggested cell width (= bandwidth) centred mode density. narrower bar means finer grid gentler thinning; wider bar means coarser grid aggressive thinning. use Sheather–Jones rest analysis:
code: res_sj       <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "sheather-jones") res_silverman <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "silverman") res_scott    <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "scott")  # Side-by-side comparison: one column per selector, one row per variable, # values in z-score units (we scaled the data in prepare_bean()). cbind(   sheather_jones = res_sj$suggested_resolution,   silverman      = res_silverman$suggested_resolution,   scott          = res_scott$suggested_resolution ) ##       sheather_jones  silverman      scott ## bio1     0.055443572 0.17774967 0.20934961 ## bio12    0.004124131 0.01304209 0.01536068 ## bio15    0.005982760 0.02203666 0.02595429 plot(res_sj) plot(res_silverman) plot(res_scott) chosen_res <- res_sj$suggested_resolution chosen_res ##        bio1       bio12       bio15  ## 0.055443572 0.004124131 0.005982760

title: Step 2 — Environmental thinning with bean
text: bean ships two thinning strategies: thin_env_nd() — stochastic. Builds grid, finds every occupied pod, randomly retains one original occurrences pod. Real coordinates GBIF metadata preserved. thin_env_center() — deterministic. Builds grid replaces points occupied pod single synthetic point centre pod. Output reproducible without seed, points longer real observations. run comparison.   Reading plots: pale grey dots original occurrences (cloud saw E-space panel earlier); highlighted markers points survive thinning. thin_env_nd highlighted markers sit top original cloud (real points kept); thin_env_center sit regular grid points centres occupied pods (synthetic locations). Notice methods break dense cluster dominated raw E-space plot.
code: # Stochastic thinning: one randomly chosen occurrence per pod. thin_nd <- thin_env_nd(   data            = prepped,   env_vars        = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),   grid_resolution = chosen_res          # per-variable cell widths from Sheather-Jones )  # Deterministic thinning: one synthetic point at the centre of each pod. # We deliberately use a fixed, coarse resolution here (0.5 z-score units on # every axis). Because the data were scaled in prepare_bean(), 0.5 means # half a standard deviation per axis — a sensible "moderate smoothing" # choice that is easy to interpret and visualise. thin_center <- thin_env_center(   data            = prepped,   env_vars        = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),   grid_resolution = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) )  # Each `thin_*` object reports the number of input occurrences, the number # of occupied pods, the retained sample size, and stores the thinned table # in `$thinned_data`. thin_nd ## --- Bean Stochastic Thinning Results --- ##  ## Thinned 1031 original points to 80 points. ## This represents a retention of 7.8% of the data. ##  ## -------------------------------------- thin_center ## --- Bean Deterministic Thinning Results --- ##  ## Thinned 1031 original points to 42 unique grid cell centers. ## This represents a retention of 4.1% of the data. ##  ## -------------------------------------- # `plot_bean()` overlays the original data (grey, faded) and the retained # thinned points (highlighted) on the same E-space scatter. plot_bean(   original_data  = prepped,   thinned_object = thin_nd,   env_vars       = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15") ) plot_bean(   original_data  = prepped,   thinned_object = thin_center,   env_vars       = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15") )

Visualise raw ellipsoid first, 2-D (static projection onto BIO1 × BIO12) 3-D (rotatable WebGL widget):  Reading plots: 2-D, ellipse 95% confidence boundary niche projected onto BIO1 × BIO12; dots occurrence points used fit niche. 3-D, translucent mesh full ellipsoidal surface BIO1 × BIO12 × BIO15 space. text: TemporalModelR ships four model families, partition_result + (optionally) pseudoabsence_result interface swapping algorithms one-chunk change: GLM — generalised linear model (build_temporal_glm). Linear / polynomial responses, easiest interpret. GAM — generalised additive model (build_temporal_gam, via mgcv). Smooth, data-adaptive nonlinear responses still per-variable interpretable. Random forest — ensemble decision trees (build_temporal_rf, via randomForest). Captures non-linear interactions automatically; less interpretable GLM/GAM. Hypervolume — n-dimensional kernel-density envelope (build_temporal_hv, via hypervolume). Presence-— pseudoabsences needed probability threshold. fit four partition per-fold metrics directly comparable. Three (GLM, GAM, RF) consume presence/absence table; hypervolume omits pseudoabsence_result.
